source_text: OBLATRANTEM te et adversus Deum, qui unus et verus est, ore sacrilego et verbis impiis obstrepentem frequenter, Demetriane, contempseram, verecundius ac melius existimans errantis imperitiam silentio spernere, quam loquendo dementis insaniam provocare. Nec hoc sine magisterii divini auctoritate faciebam, cum scriptum sit: In aures imprudentis noli quicquam dicere, ne, quando audierit, irrideat sensatos sermones tuos. Et iterum: Noli respondere imprudenti ad imprudentiam ejus, ne similis fias illi. Et sanctum quoque jubeamur intra conscientiam nostram tenere, nec inculcandum porcis et canibus exponere, loquente Domino et dicente: Ne dederitis sanctum canibus, neque miseritis margaritas vestras ante porcos, ne inculcent eas pedibus, et conversi elidant vos. Nam, cum ad me saepe, studio magis contradicendi quam voto discendi, venires, et, clamosis vocibus personans, malles tua impudenter ingerere quam nostra patienter audire, ineptum videbatur congredi tecum, quando facilius esset et levius turbulenti maris concitos fluctus clamoribus retundere quam tuam rabiem tractatibus coercere. Certe et labor irritus et nullus effectus, offerre lumen caeco, sermonem surdo, sapientiam bruto; cum nec sentire brutus possit, nec caecus lumen admittere, nec surdus audire. Haec considerans, saepe conticui, et impatientem patientia vici, cum nec docere indocilem possem, nec impium religione comprimere, nec furentem lenitate cohibere. Sed enim, cum dicas plurimos conqueri quod bella crebrius surgant, quod lues, quod fames saeviant, quodque imbres et pluvias serena longa suspendant nobis imputari, tacere ultra non oportet; ne jam non verecundiae sed diffidentiae esse incipiat quod tacemus, et dum criminationes falsas contemnimus refutare, videamur crimen agnoscere. Respondeo igitur et tibi, Demetriane, pariter et caeteris quos tu forsitan concitasti, et adversum nos odia tuis maledicis vocibus seminando, comites tibi plures radicis atque originis tuae pullulatione fecisti; quos tamen sermonis nostri admittere credo rationem: nam qui ad malum motus est mendacio fallente, multo magis ad bonum movebitur veritate cogente. Dixisti per nos fieri et quod nobis debeant imputari omnia ista quibus nunc mundus quatitur et urgetur, quod dii vestri a nobis non colantur. Qua in parte, quia ignarus divinae cognitionis et veritatis alienus es, illud primo in loco scire debes, senuisse jam mundum, non illis viribus stare quibus prius steterat, nec vigore et robore eo valere quo antea praevalebat. Hoc etiam, nobis tacentibus et nulla de Scripturis sanctis praedicationibusque divinis documenta promentibus, mundus ipse jam loquitur et occasum sui rerum labentium probatione testatur. Non hyeme nutriendis seminibus tanta imbrium copia est, non frugibus aestate torrendis solis tanta flagrantia est, nec sic vernante temperie sata laeta sunt, nec adeo arboreis foetibus autumna foecunda sunt. Minus de effossis et fatigatis montibus eruuntur marmorum crustae, minus argenti et auri opes suggerunt exhausta jam metalla, et pauperes venae breviantur in dies singulos et decrescunt, deficit in arvis agricola, in mari nauta, miles in castris, innocentia in foro, justitia in judicio, in amicitiis concordia, in artibus peritia, in moribus disciplina. Putasne tantam posse substantiam rei senescentis existere quantum prius potuit novellu adhuc et vegeta juventa pollere? Minuatur necesse est quicquid fine jam proximo in occidua et extrema devergit. Sic sol in occasu suo radios minus claro et igneo splendore jaculatur; sic, declinante jam cursu, exoletis cornibus luna tenuatur, et arbor quae fuerat ante viridis et fertilis, arescentibus ramis fit postmodum sterili senectute deformis; et fons qui, exundantibus prius venis, largiter profluebat, senectute deficiens, vix modico sudore distillat. Haec sententia mundo data est, haec Dei lex est, ut omnia orta occidant et aucta senescant, et infirmentur fortia, et magna minuantur, et cum infirmata et diminuta fuerint, finiantur. Christianis imputas quod minuantur singula, mundo senescente. Quid si et senes imputent Christianis quod minus valeant in senectute, quod non perinde ut prius vigeant auditu aurium, cursu pedum, oculorum acie, virium robore, succo viscerum, mole membrorum; et cum olim ultra octingentos et nongentos annos vita hominum longaeva procederet, vix nunc possit ad centenarium numerum perveniri? Canos videmus in pueris, capilli deficiunt antequam crescant; nec aetas in senectute desinit, sed incipit a senectute. Sic in ortu adhuc suo ad finem nativitas properat; sic quodcumque nunc nascitur, mundi ipsius senectute degenerat: ut nemo mirari debeat singula in mundo coepisse deficere, quando totus ipse jam mundus in defectione sit et in fine.
pass_a_gloss: I had frequently despised you, Demetrianus, because you, with sacrilegious mouth and impious words, were often speaking against God, who is one and true. I considered it more proper to scorn the ignorance of the erring in silence rather than to provoke the madness of the demented by speaking. I was not doing this without the authority of divine teaching, since it is written: Do not say anything in the ears of the imprudent, lest, when he hears, he ridicules your sensible words. And again: Do not respond to the imprudent according to his imprudence, lest you become similar to him. We are also commanded to keep the holy within our conscience and not to cast pearls before swine and dogs, with the Lord speaking and saying: Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet and turn to attack you. For when you came to me often, more with the intention of contradicting than of learning, and, with loud voices, preferred to impudently assert your own opinions rather than patiently listen to ours, it seemed foolish to engage with you, since it would be easier and less troublesome to calm the turbulent waves of a stormy sea with shouts than to restrain your rage with discussions. Certainly, it is a useless labor and has no effect to offer light to the blind, a sermon to the deaf, or wisdom to the brutish, since the brutish cannot perceive, the blind cannot admit light, and the deaf cannot hear. Considering these things, I often kept silent and overcame the impatient with patience, since I could neither teach the unteachable nor restrain the impious with religion nor calm the furious with gentleness. But when you say that many complain that wars arise more frequently, that plagues and famines rage, and that long periods of fair weather are interrupted by rains and showers, it is no longer proper to remain silent, lest our silence begin to be seen not as modesty but as diffidence, and while we disdain to refute false accusations, we seem to acknowledge the crime. I respond, therefore, to you, Demetrianus, and to the others whom you may have stirred up against us with your slanderous words, sowing hatred; although you have made many companions for yourself from the root and origin of your own proliferation, I believe that they will accept the reason of our words, for whoever is moved to evil by deceit will be moved to good by compelling truth. You said that through us these things happen, and that we should be blamed for all the things by which the world is now shaken and troubled, because your gods are not worshiped by us. In this matter, since you are ignorant of divine knowledge and alien to the truth, you should first know that the world has already grown old and does not stand with the same strength as before, nor does it prevail with the same vigor and power. This is also testified by the world itself, even if we remain silent and do not produce any documents from the holy Scriptures and divine preachings. The world itself now speaks and proves its own decline with the evidence of its failing things. There is not as much abundance of rain to nourish the seeds in winter, nor as much heat of the sun to dry the crops in summer, nor are the sown fields as fertile in spring, nor is autumn as fruitful with the harvest of trees. Less marble is extracted from the excavated and exhausted mountains, less wealth of silver and gold is produced, since the metals are now exhausted, and the poor veins are shortened and decreased day by day. The farmer is lacking in the fields, the sailor on the sea, the soldier in the camp, innocence in the forum, justice in judgment, concord in friendships, skill in arts, and discipline in morals. Do you think that such a great substance of a declining thing can exist as it once could when it was still new and flourishing in its youth? It is necessary that whatever is already near its end and is declining must decrease. Thus, the sun, when it sets, throws its rays with less clear and fiery splendor; thus, the moon, when its course is already declining, is diminished with worn-out horns; and the tree, which was once green and fertile, becomes sterile and deformed in its old age, with withering branches. And the spring, which once flowed abundantly with overflowing veins, now, in its old age, barely trickles with a small flow. This is the sentence given to the world, this is the law of God, that all things that arise must decline, and all things that grow must become old, and the strong must become weak, and the great must decrease, and when they have become weak and decreased, they must come to an end. You blame the Christians for the fact that individual things are decreasing, while the world is growing old. What if the old also blame the Christians for the fact that they are less strong in old age, that they do not thrive as much as before in hearing, walking, sight, strength, and bodily vigor; and whereas human life once lasted for eight or nine hundred years, it can now hardly reach the number of a hundred? We see gray hair in children, and their hair falls out before it even grows; nor does age end in old age, but rather begins with old age. Thus, in its very birth, humanity hastens to its end; thus, whatever is now born degenerates due to the old age of the world itself: so that no one should be surprised that individual things in the world have begun to fail, when the whole world is already in decline and at its end.

bible_refs.note: Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine

pass_b_english: I have often despised you, Demetrianus, because with sacrilegious mouth and impious words you have repeatedly spoken against God, who is one and true. I judged it more proper and better to spurn the ignorance of the erring in silence than to provoke the madness of the demented by speaking. I did not do this without the authority of divine teaching, since it is written: "Do not speak in the hearing of a fool, for he will despise the good sense of your words" (Proverbs 23:9). And again: "Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest you be like him yourself" (Proverbs 26:4). We are also commanded to keep what is holy within our conscience and not to cast pearls before swine and dogs, the Lord speaking and saying: "Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you" (Matthew 7:6). For you often came to me more intent on contradicting than on learning, and with loud voices you preferred to thrust your opinions forward impudently rather than listen patiently to ours. It seemed pointless to engage with you, since it would be easier and less trouble to calm the raging waves of a storm-tossed sea with shouts than to restrain your fury with reasoned words. It is surely useless labor and without effect to offer light to the blind, a discourse to the deaf, or wisdom to the brute, for the brute cannot perceive, the blind cannot receive light, and the deaf cannot hear. Reflecting on this, I have often held my peace and overcome the impatient with patience, since I could neither teach the unteachable nor restrain the impious by religion nor calm the furious by gentleness.

But now, since you say that many complain that wars break out more frequently, that plague and famine rage, and that long spells of fair weather are broken by rains and showers, and that these are imputed to us, it is no longer right to remain silent, lest our silence begin to look not like modesty but like diffidence, and while we disdain to refute false charges, we seem to acknowledge the crime. I therefore answer you, Demetrianus, and equally those others whom you may have stirred up against us, sowing hatred against us with your slanderous words, and so making many companions for yourself from the root and stock of your own kind. Yet I believe they will accept the reasoning of our words, for whoever is moved to evil by deceit will be moved all the more to good by compelling truth. You said that these things happen through us, and that all the things by which the world is now shaken and hard-pressed should be blamed on us, because your gods are not worshiped by us. In this matter, because you are ignorant of divine knowledge and a stranger to the truth, you ought first to know that the world has already grown old; it does not stand with the strength it once had, nor does it prevail with the vigor and power it formerly possessed. The world itself testifies to this even if we keep silent and produce no evidence from the holy Scriptures and divine preaching. The world itself now speaks and proves its own decline by the evidence of its failing elements. There is not the same abundance of rain in winter to nourish the seeds, nor the same scorching heat of the sun in summer to ripen the crops; the sown fields are not as joyful in the spring, nor is autumn as fruitful with the yield of trees. Less marble is quarried from the excavated and exhausted mountains; less wealth of silver and gold is brought forth, since the mines are now exhausted, and the poor veins dwindle and shrink day by day. The farmer is lacking in the fields, the sailor on the sea, the soldier in the camp, innocence in the forum, justice in the court, concord in friendships, skill in the arts, discipline in morals. Do you think the substance of a declining thing can remain as great as it was when it was still new and flourishing in youth? Whatever is already near its end and verging toward the west and the extreme must diminish. Thus the sun at its setting casts its rays with less clear and fiery splendor; thus the moon, as its course declines, is diminished with worn horns; and the tree that was once green and fertile becomes sterile and deformed by sterile old age as its branches wither. And the spring that once flowed abundantly with overflowing veins, failing with age, now barely trickles with a scant flow. This is the decree appointed for the world, this is the law of God: that all things that arise must decline, and all things that increase must grow old, the strong must become weak, the great must diminish, and when they have become weak and diminished, they must come to an end. You blame Christians because individual things diminish while the world grows old. What if the old also blamed Christians because they are less strong in old age, that they do not thrive as before in hearing, in stride, in keenness of sight, in strength of limbs, in vigor of organs, in bulk of members? And whereas human life once extended beyond eight or nine hundred years, now it can scarcely reach the number of a hundred. We see gray hair in children; hair falls out before it grows. Nor does life end in old age; rather it begins from old age. Thus even in its very birth, nature hastens to its end; thus whatever is now born degenerates because of the old age of the world itself, so that no one should marvel that individual things in the world have begun to fail, when the whole world itself is already in decline and at its end.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful prose translation, and Pass B provides a polished version with correct scripture citations (Proverbs 23:9, Proverbs 26:4, Matthew 7:6) that correspond to the Latin allusions. All clauses, including the complex descriptions of natural decay and human aging, are preserved in both versions.

source: 'OBLATRANTEM te et adversus Deum, qui unus et verus est, ore sacrilego et verbis impiis obstrepentem frequenter, Demetriane, contempseram', English: 'I had frequently despised you, Demetrianus, because you, with sacrilegious mouth and impious words, were often speaking against God, who is one and true.'
